rewritten_text:
"Surely you don't mean—" my sister began.

"Yes, I do, ma'am," Pumblechook said. "But wait a moment. Continue, Joseph. Well done! Keep going!"

"What would everyone here say," Joe asked, "to twenty pounds?"

"Generous," my sister answered.

"Well, then," said Joe, "it's more than twenty pounds."

That contemptible hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and gave a patronizing laugh. "More than that, ma'am. Good again! Keep her guessing, Joseph!"

"To finish the story, then," Joe said, delightedly passing the bag to my sister, "it's twenty-five pounds."

"Twenty-five pounds, ma'am," echoed that lowest of frauds, Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand. "And no more than you deserve, as I said when they asked my opinion. May the money bring you happiness!"

Had the villain stopped there, his conduct would have been bad enough. Instead, he deepened his guilt by taking me into custody with a claim of patronage that made all his earlier crimes seem insignificant.

"Now, Joseph and your wife," he said, gripping my arm above the elbow, "I'm the sort who always finishes what he starts. This boy must be apprenticed immediately. That's my way: apprenticed immediately."

"Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook," my sister said, clutching the money, "we owe you a great deal."

"Don't trouble about me, ma'am," replied the diabolical grain merchant. "A pleasure is a pleasure anywhere in the world. But we must get this boy apprenticed. To tell you the truth, I promised I'd attend to it."

The magistrates were sitting in the nearby Town Hall, so we went straight over to have my apprenticeship to Joe formally registered before them. I say we went; in reality Pumblechook pushed me along as though I had just picked someone's pocket or set a haystack alight. Indeed, people in court generally assumed I had been caught in the act. As he shoved me through the crowd, I heard some ask, "What's he done?" Others said, "Young, too—but he looks wicked, doesn't he?" Someone with a kindly, gentle face even handed me a religious pamphlet titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL. Its woodcut showed a sinister young man wrapped in enough chains to stock a sausage shop.

The Hall struck me as a strange place. Its pews were higher than a church's, and people leaned over them to watch. Mighty magistrates—one with powdered hair—reclined in chairs with folded arms, took snuff, fell asleep, wrote, or read newspapers. Shiny black portraits hung on the walls, looking to my artistically untrained eyes as though they had been made from brittle toffee and adhesive plaster.

"I swear," he exclaimed, "by the sun, by heaven's blue expanse, and by the flame of love consuming my heart, that if you satisfy my plea, you shall never see me again while these endure. Return home and begin your work. I shall follow its progress with anxiety beyond expression; and be assured that when you are prepared, I will come."

With those words he left me abruptly, perhaps fearing that I might alter my resolve. I watched him race down the mountain faster than an eagle flies, until the rising and falling waves of the sea of ice soon hid him.

His narrative had filled the entire day, and the sun stood at the horizon's edge when he departed. I knew I must hurry down into the valley before darkness surrounded me, yet my heart was burdened and my feet moved slowly. Finding my way along the narrow mountain paths and securing each foothold proved bewildering, so absorbed was I in the feelings awakened by that day's events. Night was well advanced by the time I reached the halfway shelter and sat beside the fountain. Stars appeared and vanished as clouds drifted across them. Dark pines towered before me, with a fallen, shattered tree lying here and there upon the earth. The scene possessed an extraordinary solemnity and stirred unfamiliar thoughts within me. I wept bitter tears and, pressing my hands together in anguish, cried, "O stars, clouds, and winds, you are all preparing to mock me! If you truly pity me, extinguish feeling and remembrance; reduce me to nothing. Otherwise, go away, go away, and abandon me to darkness."

These thoughts were desperate and wild. Yet I cannot convey how heavily the stars' everlasting glitter oppressed me, or how I heard each gust as though it were a grim, hateful sirocco coming to devour me.

Dawn had broken before I reached Chamounix. Without resting, I continued directly to Geneva. Even within myself I could find no words for my feelings. They pressed upon me with the weight of a mountain, their very excess crushing the agony beneath them. In this condition I arrived home, entered the house, and appeared before my family. My gaunt, distracted appearance caused profound alarm, but I answered none of their questions and scarcely spoke at all. I felt condemned beneath a curse, without any right to their compassion, as though I could never again share their companionship.

"Stop the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the port! Ahead on the starboard! Stop her! Let the outside wheel turn slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that bowline out! Quickly now! Come on, put out the spring line—what are you doing there? Loop the slack around that stump! Ready with the gangplank—let it down! Finished with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH'T! S'H'T! SH'T!" He was testing the steam valves.

Tom kept whitewashing, ignoring the steamboat entirely. Ben stared at him for a moment. "Ha! You're in a fix, aren't you?"

Tom gave no answer. He inspected his latest stroke with an artist's eye, gently swept the brush across again, and studied the result. Ben came up beside him. The apple made Tom's mouth water, but he stayed focused on the fence.

"Hello, old fellow. They making you work?" Ben said.

Tom suddenly turned.

"Oh, it's you, Ben! I hadn't noticed."

"Listen, I'm going swimming. Don't you wish you could come? But naturally you'd rather work, wouldn't you? Of course you would!"

Tom considered him for a moment.

"What do you mean by work?"

"Well, isn't that work?"

Tom went back to whitewashing and answered casually,

"Maybe it is, maybe it isn't. All I know is that Tom Sawyer likes it fine."

"Oh, come on. You can't pretend you're enjoying it!"

The brush kept moving.

"Enjoying it? I don't see why I shouldn't. How often does a boy get the chance to whitewash a fence?"

That gave Ben a different view of things. He stopped biting his apple. Tom moved the brush delicately back and forth, stepped away to assess his work, added a touch here and another there, and examined it again. Ben followed every movement, growing increasingly interested and absorbed. At last he said,

"Hey, Tom, let me do a little."

Tom thought about it and seemed ready to agree, then changed his mind.

"No, I don't think I can, Ben. Aunt Polly is terribly particular about this fence because it's right on the street. If it were the back fence, neither of us would mind. But she's very particular about this one. It has to be done carefully. I doubt one boy in a thousand—maybe two thousand—could do it properly."

"Really? Come on, just let me try. Only a little. I'd let you if our places were switched, Tom."

"Ben, honestly, I'd like to. But Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, and she said no. Sid wanted to do it too, and she wouldn't let him either.
